title: The Archive of Small Betrayals
text:
Writing a memoir, I discovered, is less an act of remembering than an act of negotiation with one's own vanity. The past does not arrive in tidy chapters; it surfaces in fragments, each one tinted by the mood of the present day. My mother, for instance, appears in my early drafts as a saint, but a letter I found in a shoebox revealed a woman who was often exhausted, sharp-tongued, and quietly furious at her circumstances. Rendering her honestly meant abandoning the flattering portrait I had been so carefully polishing.

The ethical question that follows is considerably thornier. Creative nonfiction demands that the writer reconstruct dialogue, compress years into paragraphs, and sometimes invent a detail to make a scene breathe. Readers accept this covenant only as long as the author remains transparent about where memory ends and craft begins. Some critics argue that any admission of invention dissolves the authority of the text, whereas others contend that candour about uncertainty is precisely what gives a memoir its credibility.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, where did the writer find a letter that changed the portrait of their mother?
options: In a letter sent by a friend

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what must creative nonfiction writers do to make a scene breathe?
options: Quote every conversation word for word
Publish their sources in an appendix

questions.text: Why did the writer initially portray their mother as a saint?
options: Because the writer wanted to flatter their own image as a child of a devoted parent
Because the writer had never read any letters written by the mother
Because the mother had asked the writer to describe her that way in print
Because critics demanded an idealised view of parents in memoirs

questions.text: What can be inferred about the author's view of memoir as a genre?
options: They believe memoir should avoid any emotional content
They believe memory is reliable only when supported by documents
They believe honesty about the limits of memory can strengthen a memoir
They believe readers should not trust any personal narrative

paragraph_translations: Escrever uma memória, descobri, é menos um ato de lembrar do que uma negociação com a própria vaidade. O passado não chega em capítulos organizados; ele surge em fragmentos, cada um tingido pelo humor do dia presente. Minha mãe, por exemplo, aparece nos meus primeiros rascunhos como uma santa, mas uma carta que encontrei numa caixa de sapatos revelou uma mulher frequentemente exausta, de língua afiada e silenciosamente furiosa com suas circunstâncias. Retratá-la com honestidade significou abandonar o retrato lisonjeiro que eu vinha polindo com tanto cuidado.

A questão ética que se segue é consideravelmente mais espinhosa. A não ficção criativa exige que o escritor reconstrua diálogos, comprima anos em parágrafos e, às vezes, invente um detalhe para que a cena ganhe vida. Os leitores aceitam esse pacto apenas enquanto o autor permanecer transparente sobre onde a memória termina e onde começa a técnica. Alguns críticos argumentam que qualquer admissão de invenção dissolve a autoridade do texto, enquanto outros sustentam que a franqueza sobre a incerteza é justamente o que confere credibilidade a uma memória.
